rv.q: The imperfections of Hilma don’t diminish its aspirations or its strange beauties.
The twists and turns in this well-composed, self-contained drama make even the slower bits engaging.
I found these moments bewildering at first, and then, as the superb cast invests them with manic energy, exhilarating.
Lucy Kirkwood's sometimes bewildering and always fascinating new play 'The Welkin' opened Wednesday at the Atlantic Theater Company.
The Welkin offers an intriguing exploration of women from here to maternity.
Its quirks notwithstanding, “The Welkin” offers an engaging and sobering reminder that even if biology is no longer destiny for women (in our culture, at least), progress remains incomplete.
While not a perfectly crafted legal drama, The Welkin is a timely reminder that we're all subject to the context in which we live.
Benson’s sturdy, propulsive staging supports a stage full of obscenely gifted performers.

But when the play resumes after intermission, Kirkwood's skillful juggling of style and substance breaks down into a puzzling second act that loses its way by emphasizing style over substance, mired down by a series of melodramatic revelations.

Although The Welkin serves distinctly familiar goods, at least it may cause viewers today to think about how far attitudes involving women have changed since 1986 when the astronomical phenomenon last passed the Earth.
What The Welkin lacks in subtlety it over-compensates for in length.
Lucy Kirkwood's text and Sarah Benson's direction offer a convoluted, histrionic, and less-than-dense treatment of an important topic.

cn.t: Kirkwood's ambitious period drama about women's subjugation divides critics between those captivated by its dark exploration of motherhood and those who find it overlong and heavy-handed, though most praise the ensemble performances.
